title: Roblox argues 8-year-old waived rights to sue in wrongful death lawsuit
text:
Roblox argues 8-year-old waived rights to sue in wrongful death lawsuit
USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect//August 19, 2026//
In Brief
Robloxfiles motion to compelarbitrationin wrongful death case.- Audree Heine allegedly exposed to harmful content on Roblox and
Discord. - Over 150 similar cases filed against Roblox in
federal court.
Can an 8-year-old waive their rights to sue a company by clicking a box?
That’s the stance of Roblox, an online gaming platform that bills itself as a digital playground.
The argument comes as the $41 billion company is embroiled in a lawsuit with the family of a Northern Kentucky child whose death by suicide, her mother says, is related to use of the platform.
Jaimee Seitz filed a wrongful death lawsuit in October 2025 alleging her daughter, Audree Heine, was exposed to “harmful and violent influences” after joining Roblox at age 8, despite Seitz setting parental controls on Audree’s account. Like many users of the gaming platform, Audree also joined Discord and TikTok to communicate with other Roblox users, where social pressures allegedly “heightened,” the suit charges, also naming the two social platforms as defendants.
In December 2024, one week after her 13th birthday and just as she began to teach herself a Nirvana song on her new guitar, Audree died by suicide. Her clothes were laid out for school the next day.
Law enforcement investigators would later find her journal that showed she allegedly was introduced to a violent subculture through the platforms, according to the lawsuit.
Roblox, Discord and TikTok all answered in federal court that the claims should be dismissed. Discord claimed Audree is bound, in part, because she entered an adult birthdate when she registered at age 8. Roblox claimed if the case does proceed, it should only be with “limited discovery.” TikTok claims it did not “proximately cause” Audree’s death.
Roblox and Tiktok and the companies’ attorneys did not provide a comment for this story.
A Discord spokesperson sent the following statement:
“Discord is deeply committed to user safety, and we want our communications platform to be the best place for friends to connect before, during and after playing games. Our terms require all users to be at least 13 to use Discord, and unlike social media platforms that use algorithms to select content and maximize engagement, our service strives to enable organic, real-time interaction and connection.
“We use a combination of advanced technology and trained safety teams to proactively find and remove content that violates our policies. We maintain strong systems intended to prevent the spread of sexual exploitation and grooming on our platform and also work with other technology companies and safety organizations to improve online safety across the internet. In addition, the Discord Family Center empowers parents and guardians with tools to help their teen have a safer experience online while maintaining privacy.”
In new documents filed this month in federal court, all three companies filed motions to dismiss the lawsuit. Roblox also filed a motion to compel arbitration, claiming Audree and her parents waived her right to a trial no less than 28 times, including “by creating her Roblox account, by accepting updates to Roblox’s Terms (six times), by using and redeeming Roblox gift cards (twice), and by purchasing Roblox’s virtual currency on Roblox (19 times).”
Robux is virtual currency — that can be bought with real money — used in Roblox to buy things like new clothes and accessories for a user’s avatar.
“Roblox made the Terms plain and Audree repeatedly manifested her assent, as courts have routinely held in examining similar agreements and as the one at issue here,” Roblox’s attorneys wrote in its motion to compel arbitration.
Seitz read a letter to The Courier Journal she wrote following Roblox’s Aug. 7 motion.
“So let’s be serious about an argument that if my child clicking a tiny ‘I agree’ box somehow means she knowingly agreed to arbitration,” Seitz said. “She was a child, she didn’t understand arbitration. She didn’t understand contracts. She didn’t understand what the little box could mean years later. But now they want a court to treat that click as though an 8-year-old knowingly negotiated away her right to have these issues heard. It’s insulting.”
Roblox’s motion, filed with Judge David Bunning in the Eastern District of Kentucky, alleges Audree agreed to arbitration when she agreed to the company’s terms of agreement. Alex Walsh, Seitz’s attorney, said that Roblox claims Audree gave up her right to a jury trial and could only pursue actions through a “secret arbitration process,” as laid out in the company’s terms of agreement.
“Why would the companies want that? For a very simple reason,” Walsh said. “They do not want the truth about how dangerous their platforms are to come out. They don’t want there to be a light shined on what they’ve done wrong and how many children have been harmed.”
Audree’s wrongful death case is just one of more than 150 cases currently against the company. Walsh said there are 10 law firms who have filed mass tort claims, all in federal court in the Northern District of California, against the company for children who have suffered similar harm. The attorneys of Walsh’s firm, Anapol Weiss, are also reviewing more than 1,000 other claims from parents nationwide regarding alleged abuse suffered by children while gaming on the platform.
Roblox has repeatedly said it focuses on a “safe environment,” according to interviews with media outlets quoted in the suit.
The latest fillings all come within days of a congressional committee launching an investigation into Roblox regarding child safety.
“If these companies believe they did nothing wrong, then they should defend it in court,” Seitz said. “Do not hide behind an agreement that an 8-year-old never understood.”
What is Roblox?
Roblox is the most downloaded game globally, according to Qustodio, a parental control company cited in the lawsuit. The platform, which includes thousands of “experiences” or games that are often designed by other users, rapidly increased in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic. An average Roblox user spends 139 minutes a day on the app, according to Qustodio’s research, also cited in the suit.
Roblox’s 2023 Annual Report showed an average of 68.5 million daily active users, including 21% under 9 years of age and 41% over 17 years of age.
While Roblox does say a child must have parental permission before signing up for an account, there is no requirement “to confirm or document” parental permission, “no matter how young a child is,” according to the suit.
Roblox’s sign-up screen states, “By clicking sign up, you agree to the Terms of Use, including the arbitration clause and you are acknowledging the Privacy Policy.”
“What we’re really fighting for is better age verification, better identity verification,” Walsh said.
Until November 2024, the game allowed anyone to “friend” and chat with anyone, regardless of age. Now, under Roblox’s default settings, adults cannot directly message children under 13, according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit also asserts for more than a decade, Roblox CEO David Baszucki and other C-suite level executives have touted the platform’s safety. Baszucki stated the platform takes “every precaution possible to make sure kids are protected from inappropriate and offensive individuals, as well as from indecent and distasteful content,” according to a 2013 interview with Wired, a technology magazine.
Discord, a communication app, and TikTok, a social media app, are also named in Seitz’s lawsuit. Discord became an app for gamers to communicate while playing. Its popularity also was driven, in part, by the pandemic. The lawsuit claims Discord “knowingly causes and facilitates grooming children for violence” and that Audree’s exposure to “homophobic and violent content exacerbated her feelings of isolation and despair.”
Discord also claims that Audree agreed to arbitration when she agreed to the app’s terms at least five times. TikTok asserted: “The balance of the Complaint’s TikTok allegations address the platform generally and do not mention Audree.”
What does the lawsuit claim?
Filed in October 2025 against Roblox and Discord and then amended in December to add TikTok, the lawsuit claims Audree was exposed to “harmful and violent influences” on the platforms.
The lawsuit alleges Seitz “trusted” the safety and community standards kept the platform “safe for children,” and Seitz set parental controls on her daughter’s account “believing that would ensure safety.”
Instead, the suit claims, Audree was bullied and felt socially isolated as other users “exploit(ed) Audree’s emotional vulnerabilities with violent rhetoric, manipulation and social pressure.”
Seitz is suing all three companies on nine claims: fraudulent concealment and misrepresentation, negligent misrepresentations, negligence regarding failure to warn and unreasonable design, negligent undertaking, strict liability regarding design defect and failure to warn, and wrongful death.
The suit also demands a jury trial regarding all of the issues. Seitz’s attorneys now have 30 days to respond to the companies’ motions.
“If you’re going to operate what you want to call this generation or the next generation’s playground, you should be so, so careful about who you’re going to let on the playground,” Walsh said.
Who is Audree Heine?
Audree Heine dreamed of being a costume designer.
The middle schooler, who lived in Boone County, used to beg her mom to bring home craft supplies from her job with the activity department of an assisted living center.
“All the time, I’d get text messages before I’d leave work, like, ‘Mom, bring home glitter. Bring home blue cardstock,’“ Seitz told The Courier Journal.
Seitz, though, didn’t know that through Audree’s time on the app, she had allegedly been influenced by a community that glorified a mass school shooter, as well as other violent ideologies.
“As her mental health deteriorated, Audree recorded a countdown in her journal,” the lawsuit stated. Seitz didn’t know about the journal, which was hidden in Audree’s locker at school, or the “toxic communities and predators,” until a law enforcement officer told her a week after Audree’s death, according to the suit.
“When Audree was discovered after her suicide, her phone was by her side,” the lawsuit said. “Leading up to her suicide, she had been livestreaming her activities on TikTok.”
Kentucky state Rep. Kim Moser, R-Taylor Mills, proposed legislation during this year’s General Assembly, House Bill 686, aimed to create a trust fund using settlement money from social media lawsuits to support local mental health initiatives.
“The fact that a kid can go to a seemingly innocent site and find themselves in this dark space is not OK; that should not be allowed,” Moser told a Cincinnati TV station.
The bill was approved by the House, but did not pass out of the Senate’s committee. Moser told The Courier Journal she will fille the bill again next session.
‘A playground for predators’
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson filed a class-action lawsuit, also in the Northern District of California, claiming that Roblox mislead and omitted information regarding Roblox’s user growth, safety initiatives and financial outlook. On Aug. 7, Wilson filed a motion to allow Ohio’s public pension to take lead in the case on behalf of investors. Ohio’s Public Employees Retirement System and State Teachers Retirement System of Ohio claim they lost a combined $21.5 million after investing in the company.
“Roblox lied to investors and failed to protect children from online predators,” Wilson said in a statement.
Several other states, including Kentucky, also filed lawsuits against Roblox over child-safety concerns. Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman filed a civil suit in October 2025, the same month as Seitz’ wrongful death suit, arguing the online gaming platform exposes kids to child predators and lacks adequate security
“Our children are not safe on Roblox. Predators and criminals aren’t just lurking in the platform’s shadows; they’ve been allowed to commit their crimes out in the open,” Coleman said in a statement.” For years, Roblox has ignored this crisis so it could continue turning a profit. Our responsibility is to protect Kentucky children from online exploitation by these predators and the companies like Roblox that knowingly facilitate it.”
Kentucky’s complaint alleges violations of failure to warn parents and kids of the platform’s dangers, negligence, unjust enrichment and violations of Kentucky’s Consumer Protection Act. Coleman wanted the court to permanently block Roblox in Kentucky.
Courtney Norris, a Jefferson County mom of three, said she thought Roblox was a “safe” choice, “like a fenced-in backyard for kids gaming.”
“That is the genius, and danger, I found of Roblox — the illusion of safety it gives parents like me,” Norris said in a statement that October. “The reality is, Roblox makes it nearly impossible to police as a parent. It takes constant vigilance. Parents are doing their part, now it’s time for platforms like Roblox to do theirs.”
Earlier this year, Enough Abuse, an advocacy group for child sex abuse prevention, released a two-part series claiming Roblox was a “playground for predators” and providing resources for parents.
Then on Aug. 12, the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee’s subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Missouri, and ranking member Sen. Richard Durbin, D-Illinois, alerted Roblox’s David Baszucki, the founder, president, CEO and chair of the board of directors, that the congressional committee launched an investigation.
The letter states that in 2025, Roblox reported 65,381 instances of suspected child sexual exploitation to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, more than double the number of instances the company reported in 2024, according to NCMEC’s own data.
“Let us be clear: children on your platform are hurting,” the letter concludes. “Congress will not look the other way.”
Reporting by Stephanie Kuzydym, Louisville Courier Journal.
summary: Our terms require all users to be at least 13 to use Discord, and unlike social media platforms that use algorithms to select content and maximize engagement, our service strives to enable organic, real-time interaction and connection. Alex Walsh, Seitz’s attorney, said that Roblox claims Audree gave up her right to a jury trial and could only pursue actions through a “secret arbitration process,” as laid out in the company’s terms of agreement.
